title: VPC attachment, egress & DNS design notes
content:
Context:
This is a working set of design notes for customer POCs where we need to attach customer VPCs to Redwood Private control plane and inference endpoints. Focus areas: connectivity patterns (peering vs Transit vs PrivateLink), ingress/egress choices, DNS resolution across accounts/VPCs, and endpoint policies. These notes are specifically tuned for mid-sized enterprise POCs (multi-account AWS) with strict data egress constraints and a requirement for predictable latency.

Goals and constraints observed across POCs:
- No public internet egress for inference requests or model artifacts unless explicitly approved by customer compliance.
- Support multi-AZ low-latency path to dedicated inference fleet (ALB/NLB to GPU hosts).
- Minimal operational friction for customer networking teams; prefer patterns they already understand (VPC peering, Transit Gateway).
- Avoid overlapping IP spaces; provide mitigation steps when overlap exists.
- DNS: split-horizon for service discovery + conditional forwarding for Route53 private zones.

Summary of connectivity options (tradeoffs):
1) VPC Peering (cross-account, region)
   - Pros: straightforward, supports native IP routing, low latency, no additional managed service cost.
   - Cons: N-to-N scaling pain for many customers, no transitive routing (unless Transit GW used), requires careful route table setup.
   - When to use: single-customer, single-VPC attachments or small POC with limited VPCs.

2) AWS Transit Gateway (TGW)
   - Pros: scales to many VPCs/accounts, supports centralized inspection and routing policies, works cross-region with attachments.
   - Cons: cost for TGW + attachments; more moving parts to coordinate with customer's network team.
   - When to use: enterprise customers with many VPCs/accounts or when we need centralized route policies.

3) Interface Endpoints / AWS PrivateLink
   - Pros: very strong isolation, customer does not need to expose routing, simplifies DNS via endpoints, works across accounts with Service Name.
   - Cons: higher per-endpoint cost, more work to provision endpoint-services on our side, limited to TCP protocols.
   - When to use: customers that forbid peering/TGW or want tight security boundary; when the service can be fronted by NLB and offered as PrivateLink.

4) VPN / Direct Connect / DX Gateway
   - Pros: deterministic performance on DX; accepted by customers with compliance needs.
   - Cons: slow to provision, cost, often unnecessary for short-term POCs.
   - When to use: regulated environments requiring dedicated circuits.

Ingress and egress patterns (detailed):
A) Customer-initiated outbound to Redwood-hosted endpoints (recommended for most POCs)
   - Customer app/VM -> NAT Gateway (customer-controlled) -> public IP to Redwood hosted API or ALB with mTLS.
   - Use when customer policy allows outbound internet to specific Redwood IP ranges; easiest to operate for short POCs.
   - Additions: require allowlist of Redwood IPs, require TLS + API key or mutual TLS for extra assurance.

B) PrivateLink (Redwood as service provider)
   - Redwood publishes service behind NLB; customer creates Interface Endpoint in their VPC; traffic stays on AWS backbone.
   - DNS: customer maps endpoint private DNS to service name; we provide split-horizon guidance.
   - Works well when customer blocks any internet egress.

C) Inbound peering / routing to Redwood VPCs (Redwood-hosted inference in customer network)
   - Attach customer VPC to Redwood VPC via peering or TGW. Routes configured so that customer sends traffic directly to inference hosts.
   - Requires route table changes; security groups must be scoped correctly.
   - Consider using NLB with TLS termination on Redwood side or pass-through depending on compliance.

D) Egress inspection / proxy patterns
   - If customer requires centralized egress controls, route outbound through a proxy or firewall (e.g., Zscaler, Palo Alto VM). Provide IP allowlist and certificate fingerprints for verification.

DNS patterns and gotchas:
- Split-horizon is the common approach. Deploy a private zone in the customer's account or use conditional forwarding to a Route53 inbound resolver in Redwood account.
- If using PrivateLink with private DNS enabled, the interface endpoint will override public resolution for the service name. We must coordinate naming to avoid unexpected overrides.
- For cross-account resolution to Redwood-hosted internal names: two viable approaches:
   1) Route53 Resolver inbound endpoints in Redwood account + outbound in customer account; conditional forwarder rules so customer VPC resolves Redwood internal hostnames.
   2) Create a shared private hosted zone (Route53) and associate VPCs across accounts (requires IAM consent).
- IPv6: fewer customers use IPv6 privately; confirm at kickoff. IPv6 introduces different resolver behavior.

IP overlap handling checklist:
- Detect overlap early with a simple script (CIDR check). If overlap found:
  - Option 1: Ask customer to allocate a new /16 or /20 for POC (fastest).
  - Option 2: Use PrivateLink to avoid routing across overlapping networks.
  - Option 3: NAT translation on Redwood side (source NAT) for the session IP range — operationally heavier.

Security group and firewall guidance (Redwood-hosted endpoints):
- Principle: least privilege; allow only customer's egress CIDR(s) to the endpoint NLB on required ports (443 for TLS).
- Recommended SG rules: HTTPS from customer CIDR, allow health-checks from Redwood monitoring IP range, deny all other inbound. Outbound minimal.
- Endpoint policy for PrivateLink: restrict available API actions to a subset for POCs to minimize blast radius.

Sample route and SG snippets (text examples for engineers):
- Route table entry for peering (customer VPC)
  Destination: 10.20.0.0/16 -> Target: vpc-peer-0a1b2c3d
- Route table entry for Redwood VPC back to customer
  Destination: 10.10.0.0/16 -> Target: vpc-peak-0a1b2c3d
- Security group (NLB fronting inference)
  Inbound: TCP 443 from 10.10.0.0/16
  Inbound: TCP 10250 from Redwood-monitoring-cidr
  Outbound: 0.0.0.0/0 (managed by Redwood egress rules)

Operational runbook notes (POC run cadence):
1) Kickoff network call with customer networking + security leads. Share this doc and a short checklist.
2) Validate CIDRs, existing TGW or peering policies, and whether PrivateLink is allowed.
3) Decide attachment pattern (Peering | TGW | PrivateLink). Document in ENG ticket.
4) Set up minimal infra: NLB with cert, SG rules, and health checks.
5) Provide customer allowlist IPs (if using public egress).
6) Perform integration test: curl from customer app instance to endpoint over expected path; verify latency and traces.
7) If failures: capture tcpdump on both sides, check route tables, check resolver behavior (dig + +trace), validate endpoint policies.

Metrics and acceptance criteria for POC:
- Median p50 latency from customer app to inference endpoint < 40ms (in-region, same AZ preferred).
- No packets traversing public internet for data plane (unless explicitly approved).
- DNS resolution time < 50ms and correct A records for private endpoints.
- TLS validation and API auth succeed consistently across 1k requests.

Unresolved questions / risks to raise during next sync:
- SLA implications if we host private endpoints via PrivateLink vs peering (is there a difference in how we report downtime?).
- How do we coordinate shared hosted zones for many customers without creating a management burden? Explore automation for hosted zone associations.
- Cost tracking: provide a sample cost estimate for PrivateLink per endpoint per month vs TGW attachment cost.

Action items (near term):
- [Arjun] Draft an automation script to detect CIDR overlaps and recommend patterns (due 2024-03-15).
- [Marina] Prototype PrivateLink NLB service + minimal endpoint policy (due 2024-03-22).
- [Liam] Prepare runbook snippet for customers that request Direct Connect (include basic bandwidth and failover notes) (due 2024-03-18).

Notes to self:
- Keep examples short and copyable. Customers prefer small, tested terraform snippets.
- For workshop sessions, prepare two network diagrams: one for PrivateLink flow, another for TGW peering flow, both annotated with route table ids.
- Remember to ask about corporate proxy/egress appliances during kickoff; this is a frequent blocker.

References and helpful commands:
- Check resolver behavior: dig +short @10.0.0.2 service.internal.example.com
- Test connectivity: curl --resolve api.service:443:10.2.3.4 https://api.service/health -v
- CIDR overlap quick check (local): python3 -c 'import ipaddress,sys; print(any(ipaddress.ip_network(a).overlaps(ipaddress.ip_network(b)) for a in ["10.0.0.0/16"] for b in ["10.0.0.0/12"]))'

End of notes.

(Keeping this deliberately conversational — this doc will be turned into a short customer-facing one-pager after we validate the PrivateLink prototype.)
